findings.finding: The cap read using `git cat-file --batch-check` cannot tell a missing path from an unreadable object. Git prints `<input> missing` both when `.github/module-size-limit.txt` is absent from the tree and when the commit, root tree, or `.github` subtree can't be read (corrupt repo, or a partial clone that failed to fetch). It exits 0 either way. Today, `git ls-tree <sha> -- cap` exits non-zero on an unreadable commit or tree, which becomes Unavailable. After the change, those revisions would quietly count as 'not qualified' and could produce a wrong qualified_revisions count or cap-change events. That contradicts the plan's claim that 'a real git failure still raises and becomes `Unavailable`'.

scenarios: A repo with a corrupt or missing tree object for one in-range commit: today Unavailable, after the change silently skipped

git-cat-file docs (git-scm.com / Debian man page): if a name on stdin 'cannot be resolved to an object in the repository', cat-file ignores the custom format and prints `<object> SP missing LF`. This rule does not tell an absent path apart from an unreadable tree along the path.

Existing failure coverage test_git_metrics.py:530-535 only monkeypatches `_git` to throw RuntimeError. It does not exercise a per-object resolution failure inside a batch, so '178 passed' cannot confirm the claim.
findings.finding: The plan says that with `git cat-file --batch-check` 'a real git failure still raises and becomes `Unavailable`' and that 'Results are unchanged'. Per git's documentation, batch-check prints `<name> missing` for any name that cannot be resolved to an object. That includes a commit whose tree (or `.github` subtree) object is corrupt or absent, not just a cap file that does not exist. The current `_read_cap_at` uses `git ls-tree <sha> -- <cap>`, which exits non-zero on an unreadable tree, so `_git` raises and the result is `Unavailable`. The new design would quietly classify the same revision as not qualified. Only process-level failures (spawn error, non-zero exit, timeout) would still raise.
findings.location: Approach — `src/rebar/metrics/git_metrics.py` bullet ("`missing` stays the ordinary not-qualified case … a real git failure still raises and becomes `Unavailable`"; "Results are unchanged")
scenarios: A repository with a corrupt or missing tree object (damaged pack, interrupted fetch, or a partial or shallow clone where some in-range trees are unavailable): today `rebar metrics` reports 'git command failed while reading repository history'. After the change those revisions are dropped as not qualified, and the metric may report a misleading 'no positive-integer module-size cap' reason or a shortened cap history with no warning.
findings.suggested_fix: Two options. (1) In the same batch-check process, also send `<sha>^{tree}` for each in-range commit, and raise RuntimeError (so the result becomes `Unavailable`) if any of those lines reports `missing`. This keeps the process count at 2 and keeps today's fail-loudly behaviour for unreadable commit trees. (2) Narrow the Approach text to say per-object resolution failures are reported by git as `missing` and treated as not qualified, and stop claiming 'Results are unchanged' for that case. Either way, add a unit test that pins the chosen behaviour.

findings.finding: The plan reads every sampled revision's blobs in one `git cat-file --batch` but doesn't say to de-duplicate blob shas across samples. It does say this for the cap step ('the distinct cap blobs'). Unchanged modules keep the same blob sha across many of the up to 50 samples. Without de-duplication, one captured stdout repeats every unchanged module up to 50 times. Today each sample's output is captured and dropped one at a time. The results would still be right, because `_parse_batch_output` keys by sha, but peak memory and the size of a single 300 s-timeout call grow sharply on a real repository.

findings.finding: The root cause says the same per-revision cost hits `rebar metrics` on a long real history, and that the whole walk runs twice ('once for `cap_change_events` and once for `module_size_trend`'). Yet the plan keeps one `ls-tree -r` per qualified revision for each metric and keeps the doubled walk, without saying why. That leaves about 2N git starts on an N-commit range, which becomes the main cost after the change. The module already has a per-context cache (`_analysis_cache`/`_cached_analysis`) that the structural specs use. Through `_git_spec`, the two git specs could share one `_qualified_history` result per (repo_root, since, until), halving production starts with little code and small blast radius. The plan neither adopts this nor explains why the residual per-revision cost is acceptable.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that `_fast_import_history` writes to the branch HEAD names, either by creating the repo with an explicit initial branch or by pointing HEAD at the imported ref, so the test doesn't depend on the host's `init.defaultBranch`.
evidence: Plan: "the oracle test builds its 60-commit history with one `git fast-import` (helper `_fast_import_history`, shas from `--export-marks`)". No target ref or branch is named.
tests/unit/metrics/test_git_metrics.py:29-33: `_init` runs `git init -q` with no `-b`/`--initial-branch`, so HEAD's branch name comes from the environment.
src/rebar/metrics/git_metrics.py:183-186: `_list_commits` runs `git log --format=%H%x09%cI`, which reads from HEAD.
Evidence class: fast-import is Partially-verified. The author measured it in one sandbox, but the HEAD/ref match depends on the environment and is Unverified across CI and developer configs.
findings.finding: The plan doesn't say which ref `_fast_import_history` writes its commits to. `_init` creates the repo with a bare `git init -q`, so the branch HEAD points to depends on the host's `init.defaultBranch` (master, main, or something else). If the stream's `commit refs/heads/<x>` doesn't match that branch, HEAD stays unborn, `_list_commits` (`git log` from HEAD) fails, and the oracle test breaks on some machines but not others. The author's single-environment measurement can't rule this out.
scenarios: CI or a developer machine has `init.defaultBranch=main` while the helper hard-codes `refs/heads/master`, or the other way round. `git log` then fails on an unborn HEAD and the oracle test fails, even though it passed in the author's sandbox.
findings.suggested_fix: In the oracle test, either create the repo with an explicit initial branch (for example `git init -q -b main`, at no extra git start) and have the fast-import stream use `commit refs/heads/main`, or read the ref HEAD names from `.git/HEAD` (a file read, not a git start) and use that ref in the stream's `commit` command.
